content: The following is a professional interpretation of the provided data: 1. Molecular WHO-Approved Rapid Diagnostics for Tuberculosis (TB): The use of molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) for TB screening in people living with HIV demonstrated moderate accuracy. These tests identified 3 to 14 more true positives (patients correctly diagnosed with active TB) per 1,000 patients tested compared to symptom-based screening followed by mWRDs. False negatives (patients incorrectly classified as not having active TB) were reduced by 3 to 14 cases per 1,000 patients tested when using mWRDs. False positives (patients incorrectly classified as having active TB) increased by 8 to 10 cases per 1,000 patients tested with mWRDs compared to symptom-based screening followed by mWRDs. The specificity of mWRDs ranged from 90% to 96%, while sensitivity estimates varied from 25% to 83%, depending on the study population and context. 2. Symptom Screening for TB in Children and Adolescents: Symptom screening for TB in child and adolescent close contacts (under 15 years) showed low sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 3 to 5 true positives per 1,000 patients tested, while false negatives ranged from 1 to 11 cases per 1,000 patients. Specificity estimates ranged from 68% to 82%, with false positives ranging from 279 to 308 cases per 1,000 patients tested. Variability in sensitivity was partly attributed to studies focusing on children under 5 years of age, who may present differently. The low number of children with pulmonary TB in these studies also contributed to imprecision. 3. Chest X-Ray for TB Screening in Children and Adolescents: Chest X-ray screening for TB in child and adolescent close contacts showed moderate accuracy. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 78% to 100%, with false negatives ranging from 1 to 16 cases per 1,000 patients tested. Specificity estimates ranged from 87% to 100%, with false positives ranging from 81 to 90 cases per 1,000 patients tested. The inclusion of chest radiography as part of the composite reference standard in all studies introduced a risk of bias, and the small number of patients contributing to sensitivity analysis led to imprecision. 4. Symptom Screening in Children Living with HIV: Symptom screening for TB in children living with HIV in outpatient settings showed moderate sensitivity but low specificity. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 3 to 6 true positives per 1,000 patients tested, while false negatives ranged from 2 to 39 cases per 1,000 patients. Specificity estimates ranged from 89% to 97%, with false positives ranging from 54 to 60 cases per 1,000 patients tested. Studies had a high risk of bias in the flow and timing domain, and differences in clinical diagnostic thresholds contributed to heterogeneity. 5. Study Limitations and Variability: Many studies were conducted in high TB burden settings, and some focused on specific populations, such as inpatients, pregnant women, or individuals with low CD4 counts. These factors may limit the generalizability of findings. Variability in sensitivity and specificity estimates was observed across studies, influenced by differences in study populations, diagnostic thresholds, and reference standards. 6. Recommendations: Molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) are recommended for TB screening in people living with HIV due to their higher sensitivity compared to symptom-based screening alone. Symptom screening in children and adolescents, particularly those living with HIV, should be supplemented with additional diagnostic tools, such as chest X-rays or mWRDs, to improve diagnostic accuracy. Further research is needed to address variability and improve diagnostic strategies, particularly in pediatric and HIV-infected populations.
